identity.title: Unilateral leg swelling: calf circumference difference >3 cm (10 cm below tibial tuberosity), with calf tenderness

technique.how: With the patient supine and legs relaxed, mark a point 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity on both legs and measure calf circumference with a tape at that level. A difference >3 cm is positive (Wells item); also note whether the swollen calf is tender along the deep venous system and whether swelling is unilateral.
technique.prerequisites: Tape measure; both legs exposed and compared at the same landmark.
technique.contraindications: None; avoid forceful manipulation of a suspected thrombosed limb.

interpretation.positive_finding: Asymmetric calf diameter modestly raises the probability of DVT (pooled LR+ 1.80) and contributes one point to the Wells score; it is not diagnostic on its own.
interpretation.negative_finding: Absence of calf asymmetry (LR 0.57) or of calf swelling (LR 0.67) lowers probability slightly; neither excludes DVT, especially proximal or bilateral disease.
interpretation.pitfalls: Cellulitis, ruptured Baker cyst, muscle injury and chronic venous insufficiency also produce asymmetry; prior DVT or lymphedema causes baseline asymmetry. Measurements vary with landmark placement and tape tension.
interpretation.changes_what: Positive: add a Wells point and proceed to compression ultrasound if score moderate/high; negative: lowers score and, with a negative D-dimer, supports exclusion without imaging.

estimates.population: Adults with clinically suspected DVT in cohort studies
estimates.quote: difference in calf diameter (LR, 1.80) ... difference in calf diameter (LR, 0.57) was useful for ruling out DVT
estimates.location: Abstract, Data Synthesis (finding: difference in calf diameter; positive and absent)

estimates.target_condition: Deep vein thrombosis (imaging-confirmed); finding = calf swelling (any)
estimates.population: Adults with clinically suspected DVT in cohort studies
estimates.quote: only absence of calf swelling (LR, 0.67) or difference in calf diameter (LR, 0.57) was useful for ruling out DVT
estimates.location: Abstract, Data Synthesis (finding: absence of calf swelling)

sources.citation: Goodacre S, Sutton AJ, Sampson FC. Meta-analysis: The value of clinical assessment in the diagnosis of deep venous thrombosis. Ann Intern Med. 2005;143(2):129-139.
Wells PS, Owen C, Doucette S, Fergusson D, Tran H. Does this patient have deep vein thrombosis? JAMA. 2006;295(2):199-207.
Anand SS, Wells PS, Hunt D, Brill-Edwards P, Cook D, Ginsberg JS. Does this patient have deep vein thrombosis? JAMA. 1998;279(14):1094-1099.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not rely on calf measurement to exclude DVT in patients with bilateral swelling, prior DVT, lymphedema, or chronic venous disease where baseline asymmetry is expected.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: A tense, painful, cyanotic swollen leg (phlegmasia) or any DVT signs with dyspnea/hypoxia require urgent imaging and anticoagulation decisions the same day.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: Anand 1998 RCE: individual DVT signs have poor reliability and accuracy (clinical exam sensitivity 60-96%, specificity 20-72%); the value lies in the structured Wells score.

extraction_notes: Numbers are pooled LRs from the Goodacre 2005 abstract; CIs and sens/spec are not in the abstract and the full text is not open access, so they are null. The Goodacre finding is 'difference in calf diameter' without the exact >3 cm threshold stated in the abstract; the >3 cm cut-off is the Wells operational definition. JAMA RCE 1998/2006 abstracts do not give per-sign LRs and are cited for context and reliability statements only.
